1966 Chrysler Imperial Has the Right Combo: Unrestored, All-Original, 440 Muscle
25 photos
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug
Unrestored. Original. The factory engine is still under the hood, and it’s even working. Is this enough to convince you to check out this 1966 Chrysler ? It should be.
This Imperial Crown four-door hardtop is a little piece of American car history, as it has never been touched or restored in any way. Everything you see on this car is exactly how Chrysler’s engineers wanted to be, so whoever refreshes it would better stick with the original configuration and not convert it into a custom abomination.
That’s why this Imperial is now here. It’s trying to sell, hoping that someone out there would have the resources and the courage to return it to its day-glory. It won’t be easy, especially if sticking to the all-original setup is the long-term objective.
Finding the necessary parts is more challenging than it looks because 1966 Imperials are not that common. Donors rarely make the headlines, and when they do, they come in ridiculous condition.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The Imperial didn’t receive any significant changes for the 1966 model year. The reason was the facelift that was introduced in 1964, and which completely transformed the car. This refresh worked like a charm in the following years, and Chrysler decided to stick with only subtle changes, such as the new grille introduced in 1966.
The Imperial continued to be offered in two configurations. The crown could be ordered as a two and a four-door hardtop plus a convertible, while the Lebaron was offered only as a four-door hardtop.
While the Imperial started the decade with a 413 V8 engine rated at 340 horsepower under the hood, this unit was upgraded for the 1966 model. This was actually the biggest change that happened in 1966, as the Imperial switched to a 440 engine that produced 350 horsepower.
Chrysler’s strategy worked, at least when the 1964 facelift came out. Sales increased almost overnight, with the company ending the year with 23,285 cars shipped to American buyers. Another overhaul followed in 1967.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The first thing that caught my attention when I first spotted this Chrysler was the solid body. It still looks clean and straight, but I wouldn’t actually make an offer without seeing it in person.
Sure, it doesn’t look restored, and that’s a plus, but you just ned to inspect everything for signs of rust. If possible, you should raise the Imperial on a lift to inspect the undersides and look for signs of previous repairs. The floors are typically the first ones to be invaded by rust, and without checking out every inch of metal thoroughly, you won’t be able to tell of sure if the car is as advertised.
If it passes the metal inspection, you should go on with a verification of the cabin. It shows its age, and the front seats will require urgent fixes.
I just wish we knew more about this car’s past because it doesn’t look like the owners babied it. The cabin is the living proof, as I can’t see how the front seats would end up in this shape if the car was parked in a garage and regularly started.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The owner insists that the photos you see in the gallery perfectly showcase the condition of the car today. They must be recent images, though they also leave some questions without an answer, especially the ones regarding the car’s past.
Otherwise, you’ll get good news when you open the hood. The engine hiding in there is a 440 – as I told you, the Imperial moved to a 440 beginning with the 1966 model year, so there’s a chance that this is the original configuration that was installed by Chrysler before the vehicle left the factory.
It runs and drives, and that’s fantastic news for someone who wants to drive this car during the restoration. However, it’s unclear if the vehicle is prepared for a long journey, and my recommendation is that you send your mechanic for an inspection because this is the only way to tell if flying in and driving home is possible.
Otherwise, you should also consider the shipping costs, which could be quite high, depending on where you live.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug As for the selling price, this car isn’t expensive. The Imperial was a car whose maintenance was quite easy and affordable, but on the other hand, they burned a lot of fuel, which made sense, given the 440 engine under the hood.
They aren’t necessarily the most sought-after classics, but a collector would pay big bucks for a specimen that checks the right boxes (such as being all-original and in tip-top shape).
The owner wants $10,000 for this Imperial Crown, and they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay, which is typically a sign that you might be able to get a discount if you’re committed to a fast purchase.
The car is parked in Yucca Valley, California, and a title is also included in the sale.
